new_statements.quote: 7.2.4.1.3. Tone The following surface tones are recorded: high, low, mid, and high-falling.
new_statements.citation: Vossen, Rainer. 1982. The Eastern Nilotes: linguistic and historical reconstructions (Kölner Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 9). Berlin: Dietrich Reimer. 512 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 196, §7.2.4.1.3 'Tone' (within §7.2.4.1 'Ongamo', pp. 193-196); PDF page 4 of the Rosetta Project excerpt
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ongamo is described as a tone language with four surface tones (high, low, mid, high-falling); the same tones are recorded for Maasai, where they are lexically and grammatically relevant, and Vossen 1981 (p. 50) adds that nominal case is marked by tone in Ongamo-Maa. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent; the reading is 'tonal, silent on stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Vossen warns (p. 195) that 'linguistic data on On are still scanty' and that Heine & Vossen's material contains irregularities, and (1981: 46) that tone-marking in the comparative wordlist is 'in most cases tentative'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns surface tones on lexical items (Vossen's data conventions: nouns in the singular, verbs in the infinitive); no word-vs-phrase domain is discussed and no stress is mentioned. Data are Heine & Vossen's 1975 field notes plus Fleming 1965 and Ehret 1967/1971/1974 wordlists.
new_statements.identity_note: Ngasa = Ongamo (speakers' own name oŋgamo, sg. oŋgamoni), also Kingasa/Kingassa/Ongamoi/Shaka; Glottolog ngas1238, ISO nsg. Vossen 1982 labels it 'Ongamo (On)' and treats it as a single language with no dialect division; no identity problem.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. §7.2.4.1.3 Tone (p. 196): 'The following surface tones are recorded: high, low, mid, and high-falling.' Also notes data on Ongamo are 'still scanty' (p. 195, vowel-harmony section). Maasai section (p. 198-199) says tone matters lexically and grammatically; North Maa has three tones.

sources.note: Used only to confirm citations (Heine & Vossen 1975/76 AuÜ 59(2): 81-105; Vossen 1981 pp. 41-57; Vossen 1982; Vossen & Heine 1989 pp. 181-217). No other Ongamo-specific work by either author.

sources.note: Nothing on stress; states the Ongamo data come from Fosbrooke's early-1950s notes, Fleming's 1965 wordlist, Ehret 1967 (unpublished vocabulary), 1971, 1974a, and Heine & Vossen's Feb/Mar 1975 fieldwork (Heine & Vossen 1975-76); only two or three hundred elderly speakers.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 50: 'Nominal case is marked by tone in ONGAMO-MAA, Teso, and Turkana.' Tone-marking conventions for the comparative wordlist (high, low, high-falling, low-rising; mid unmarked) described as 'in most cases tentative'.
